report.releaseDate: 26 Oct 2026 (AiGC Market Performance Report – September 2026 edition; covers 13 Jul–30 Sep 2026)
report.currency: CAD (tables in C$ millions unless stated; ~USD alongside at USD/CAD 1.40)
report.verdict: Alberta's first 80 days as Canada's second open iGaming market produced C$2,885m (~$2,061m) of wagers and C$122.1m (~$87.2m) of non-adjusted GGR, with September alone at C$56.6m (~$40.4m) — a run-rate (~C$680m annualised) already ~1.7x the GGR implied by the government's own C$76m year-one revenue forecast. It is a casino-led market (78% of NAGGR) run on an Ontario-style conduct-and-manage model with a ~22% effective public take, cheap licences and the strictest day-one advertising rules in Canada; the swing factors from here are the Premier's threatened advertising clampdown, enforcement against the ~70% offshore base, and how 50 approved sites split a ~5m-person province.

kpis.label: Est. public take Q3 (20% of net + 3% GGR)
kpis.delta: Sep run-rate ~C$12.7m/mth vs C$76m FY1 budget

summary: **Market structure.** Alberta opened Canada's second competitive iGaming market on 13 Jul 2026 under the iGaming Alberta Act (SA 2025, Bill 48) and amended Gaming, Liquor and Cannabis Act. Alberta Gaming, Liquor and Cannabis (AGLC) is regulator and standard-setter; the new Crown corporation Alberta iGaming Corporation (AiGC) 'conducts and manages' the market and contracts private operators — a direct analogue of Ontario's AGCO/iGO split. Minimum age is 18 (Ontario: 19).

**Size (primary, unaudited).** AiGC's September Market Performance Report shows 13 Jul–30 Sep wagers of C$2,885.1m (~$2,061m), winnings C$2,762.9m (~$1,974m) and non-adjusted GGR (NAGGR = wagers less winnings, before promotional costs) of C$122.1m (~$87.2m); blended hold 4.23%. Monthly NAGGR: Jul (19 days) C$22.2m → Aug C$43.3m → Sep C$56.6m (+30.7% MoM) on wagers of C$542.9m → C$1,064.8m → C$1,277.4m (+20.0%).

**Run-rate vs forecast.** September annualises at ~C$680m (~$485m) NAGGR before further operator additions — ~1.7x the ~C$390m GGR implied by Minister Dale Nally's C$76m (~$54m) year-one government revenue forecast, and inside the C$850m–C$1.2bn year-one range third parties attribute to H2 Gambling Capital (two conflicting figures; neither read at source). Our estimate for the first 12 months is C$740–810m NAGGR (3–5% monthly growth) — see forecast.

**Online vs retail.** AiGC reports online only. The legacy AGLC estate (≈30 casinos' slots, VLTs, lottery, bingo and the state site Play Alberta) booked FY2024-25 gaming net sales of C$2,133.7m (~$1,524m) and gaming net income of C$1,486.9m (~$1,062m). Play Alberta's FY2024-25 net sales were C$269.9m (~$193m) and government estimated it held only 23–32% of provincial online play, i.e. ~70% of iGaming was offshore pre-launch. On September's run-rate, regulated online NAGGR is now ~C$680m/yr vs Play Alberta's C$270m — roughly a 2.5x step-up in onshore online revenue.

**Product mix.** Casino (RNG slots, tables, poker, keno) delivered 78.2% of Q3 NAGGR (C$95.5m, ~$68.2m), Sports & Event Betting 16.4% (C$20.1m, ~$14.4m) and Live Casino 5.4% (C$6.6m, ~$4.7m). September split: 75.6% / 19.5% / 4.9%. Fantasy Sports and Peer-to-Peer (poker/exchange) are eligible product categories but reported no activity in Q3.

**Sports betting.** Q3 handle C$325.8m (~$233m), NAGGR C$20.1m, hold 6.2%. September handle C$152.7m (+36% MoM) and NAGGR C$11.1m (+114%) at a 7.3% hold as NFL/CFL/college football returned; August hold was only 4.6%. Betting is 11–12% of wagers but 16–20% of NAGGR — higher margin, far lower turnover than casino.

**Players.** Active player accounts rose 226,959 (Jul) → 314,091 → 388,585 (Sep); ARPPA C$98 → C$138 → C$146 (~$104); wagers per account ~C$3,300/month. Accounts are not unique players (multi-operator sign-ups), so penetration cannot be computed from this series.

**Licensing regime.** Two-step entry: (1) AGLC registration per distinct iGaming site (due diligence, compliance attestations, integration with the centralised self-exclusion system), then (2) a commercial operating agreement with AiGC; betting starts only once AiGC notifies. Fees are fixed and non-refundable: C$50,000 (~$36k) one-time application (includes due-diligence costs) and C$150,000 (~$107k) annual registration per site; platform/critical-system suppliers C$15,000/yr (~$11k); other suppliers (e-wallets, oddsmakers, integrity monitors, test labs) C$3,000/yr (~$2k). Standards sit in AGLC's Standards and Requirements for Internet Gaming (SRIG, ~85 pp, Jan 2026; revised 18 Jun 2026).

**Fiscal regime (revenue share, not a tax statute).** Per Alberta.ca: 3% of gross gaming revenue is allocated first to First Nations initiatives (2%) and social-responsibility/problem-gambling funding (1%); the remaining 'net iGaming revenue' is split 80% operator / 20% province. Effective public take ≈22.4% of GGR (our estimate; the precise definition of 'net' — e.g. treatment of promotional credits and GST — is not published). Base is revenue, not turnover; no player withholding (recreational winnings untaxed in Canada).

**Public take to date (estimate).** Applying the published formula to NAGGR gives ~C$27.4m (~$19.6m) for Q3 — province C$23.7m, First Nations C$2.4m, RG C$1.2m — and ~C$12.7m in September alone (~C$152m annualised vs C$76m budgeted for year one). Treat as an upper bound: if the agreements compute the share on promo-adjusted revenue the take is lower.

**Operator landscape.** 22 sites went live on day one from 50 registered operators; active operators (with agreements and live sites) were 16/20/24 in Jul/Aug/Sep. At the 13 Oct 2026 grace-period close AiGC listed 29 operators and 50 sites, including bet365 (casino and sportsbook), FanDuel, DraftKings, BetMGM, BetRivers, Bally Bet, BetVictor, BET99, Stake (Stake Canada Ltd), Betway, JackpotCity, PlayOJO, TonyBet, PlayBetNova (Delasport) and AGLC's Play Alberta. AiGC CEO Dan Keene guides to 60+ sites in 2027. Operator-level shares are not disclosed (n/a).

**Channelisation and enforcement.** AiGC's stated goals: 70% of online activity on regulated sites after year one and 75% by year two (from ~30% pre-launch). The three-month transition ended 13 Oct 2026; unregistered sites must stop taking Alberta wagers and AGLC says it will monitor and act. Enforcement tools (payment/ISP blocking, affiliate liability) are not publicly specified — this is the key swing factor for the 70% target.

**Advertising — strictest in Canada, and tightening.** SRIG (18 Jun 2026) bans public advertising of inducements, bonuses and credits (permitted only on the operator's own site or via opted-in direct marketing); bars athletes except for responsible-gambling messaging; prohibits content appealing to minors (cartoons, influencers, celebrities), billboards near schools, 'excessive play' or financial-security claims; land-based casinos may not promote iGaming inducements. Premier Danielle Smith said on 25 Oct 2026 that Albertans are complaining about ad saturation and rule changes may follow — a live regulatory risk for Q1–Q2 2027.

**Responsible gambling.** A centralised self-exclusion system covering all iGaming sites, all land-based venues or all gambling was live from day one (Ontario still lacks this); 1% of GGR is earmarked for RG and treatment; the Premier has said operators should fund addiction treatment. AML/KYC runs to FINTRAC standards with sanctions screening, account-sharing detection and continuous geolocation.

**Payments.** AiGC publishes no deposit-method data. Payment providers and e-wallets must register with AGLC as 'supplier–other' (C$3,000/yr). Canadian regulated iGaming is Interac e-Transfer-led with cards and wallets secondary [industry norm, not quantified by the regulator]; the SRIG position on credit-card and crypto deposits was not verified in this research.

**Governance and politics.** Lead ministry is Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction (Minister Nally). AGLC is simultaneously regulator and operator of Play Alberta — a conflict flagged by trade press — and a bill tabled in May 2026 could enable a sale of the Play Alberta platform/customer data. Budget 2026 assumes AGLC gaming and lottery net income of C$1,577m (~$1,126m) in 2026-27 rising to C$1,635m by 2028-29 and total AGLC net income ~C$2.4bn/yr — land-based cannibalisation by online is not visibly modelled.

**Benchmark.** Ontario (≈3x Alberta's population) generated FY2024-25 wagers of C$82.7bn and GGR of C$3.2bn (iGO) and >C$4bn GGR in calendar 2025 on C$98.3bn wagers (+34% YoY). Alberta's September NAGGR equals roughly 17% of Ontario's monthly GGR on ~1/3 of the population — consistent with a market in month three of channelisation, with headroom as the roster fills.

**Read-through for an operator.** Fundamentals are attractive: casino-led mix, 18+ age, high-income province, ~22% effective take, negligible fee drag (C$150k ≈ 0.5% of an average operator's annualised Sep NAGGR), Ontario-compatible compliance stack and transparent monthly data. Constraints are commercial and political: 50 sites chasing ~5m people, promotions pushed only through owned channels (so NAGGR flatters net revenue), an imminent advertising review, undefined 'net revenue' base, and no operator-level data to track share. Late entrants need differentiated product (live, P2P/poker once liquidity rules settle) or Ontario scale; sports-only models face thin, volatile economics.

segments.name: Sports & event betting
segments.headline: A 16% minority product with volatile hold (4.6%→7.3%) — September's C$11.1m already exceeds Play Alberta's entire FY2024-25 sports take.
narrative: Across the 80-day period licensed books took C$325.8m (~$232.7m) of handle and kept C$20.1m (~$14.4m) of non-adjusted GGR, a blended hold of 6.2%. The monthly sequence is instructive: July's 19 days (C$60.9m handle, C$3.8m NAGGR) coincided with the final week of the World Cup and held 6.2%; August (C$112.2m handle, C$5.2m NAGGR) was a baseball-heavy, low-margin month at 4.6%; September (C$152.7m handle, +36% MoM; C$11.1m NAGGR, +114%) brought NFL, CFL and college football and a 7.3% hold. Betting's share of market NAGGR swung 17.3% → 12.1% → 19.5% while its share of wagers stayed at 11–12%, so the vertical earns roughly 1.7x casino's margin per dollar staked but on a fraction of the turnover.

The blended 6.2% hold sits below the 8–10% that parlay-heavy US books now print, which points to a straight-bet/moneyline-weighted early mix and aggressive launch pricing: because inducements may be marketed only on-site or by opted-in CRM, odds boosts and bet credits are being spent inside the apps rather than on billboards, and AiGC's 'non-adjusted' metric does not strip them out. We would expect Q4 hold to normalise toward 7–8% with the NHL (Oilers, Flames), the NFL mid-season and the Grey Cup in Calgary on 15 Nov 2026, and for betting's NAGGR share to oscillate between ~15% in quiet months and ~20% in football months.

The eligible 'Sports and Event Betting' category covers traditional sports, esports and novelty markets with single-event, live, pool and parlay bet types (single-event wagering has been lawful in Canada since the 2021 Criminal Code amendment). Peer-to-peer sports betting (exchanges) is a separate eligible category that recorded no activity in Q3 — a white space. The pre-launch baseline underlines how much sports value was offshore: Play Alberta's sports vertical generated only C$8.0m (~$5.7m) of net sales in all of FY2024-25, 3% of its total, so the open market's September alone exceeded the state monopoly's annual sports revenue.

For an operator the demographics are favourable — an 18+ age floor (Ontario is 19+) widens the young-male sports cohort — but acquisition is constrained: athletes may appear only in responsible-gambling messaging, public bonus advertising is banned, and licensees are exposed if affiliates also promote unlicensed sites, so growth leans on brand, media and league partnerships (bet365 is a CFL partner in Ontario and Alberta), sponsorship and CRM. Operator-level handle shares are not published (n/a); mature-market precedent suggests the FanDuel/DraftKings/bet365/BetMGM/theScore cohort will concentrate share, leaving sports-only challengers with thin, volatile unit economics unless they cross-sell casino.

Two regulatory items bear directly on this vertical. First, the Premier's 25 Oct comments about ad saturation were anchored in sports broadcasts, so any tightening is likely to land hardest on sportsbook marketing. Second, US-style event-contract/prediction-market products are not an Eligible iGame under the Act; whether AGLC treats such offers to Albertans as unlicensed gambling has not been addressed in any source reviewed and is a watch item.

segments.name: Online casino & live casino
segments.headline: Casino is where the value sits — 78% of NAGGR at a steady ~4.2% hold; live dealer is under-indexed at 5% and shrinking in share.
narrative: RNG casino (slots, progressive jackpots, tables, poker and keno) took C$2,275.2m (~$1,625m) of wagers and C$95.5m (~$68.2m) of NAGGR in the period, a 4.20% hold. Monthly wagers ran C$422.4m → C$849.6m (+101%) → C$1,003.2m (+18%) and NAGGR C$17.0m → C$35.7m → C$42.8m (+19.9% in September). Hold edged up 4.02% → 4.20% → 4.27%, consistent with a slots-dominant mix where high recycling of balances keeps revenue at 4–5% of turnover. Casino's share of NAGGR was 76.4% in July, peaked at 82.3% in August when sports hold collapsed, and settled at 75.6% in September.

Live casino (dealer-hosted tables, live slots/keno, gameshows) generated C$284.1m (~$203m) of wagers and C$6.6m (~$4.7m) of NAGGR at a stable 2.3% hold, but its share of market NAGGR fell 6.3% → 5.6% → 4.9% as RNG-centric brands came online. In mature online-casino markets live dealer typically captures a materially larger slice of casino GGR than 5%, so Alberta looks under-penetrated — an opening for live-led brands and for studios licensing content through AGLC-registered platform suppliers (C$15,000/yr) and test labs (C$3,000/yr).

The legacy baseline frames the channelisation story. Play Alberta's FY2024-25 casino net sales were C$197.3m (~$141m, 73% of its C$269.9m), with live dealer C$21.4m and instants C$27.8m. The open market's September casino-plus-live NAGGR of C$45.6m annualises to ~C$547m — roughly 2.5x the state site's annual casino take within three months — which, set against government's pre-launch estimate that only 23–32% of online play was regulated, indicates offshore volume is moving onshore quickly, albeit with some demand creation from 24 brands marketing simultaneously.

Unit economics for operators: public take of ~22.4% of GGR (estimate) plus federal GST plus C$150,000 per site; against that, launch-phase promotional intensity is invisible in NAGGR, and we would expect promo-adjusted revenue to run 20–35% below NAGGR in year one (analyst estimate). Blended ARPPA of C$146 (~$104) in September is dragged down by low-value sports accounts; casino ARPPA is likely higher. Poker sits inside the casino category and is confined to Alberta liquidity unless an inter-jurisdictional pooling framework emerges (the Supreme Court of Canada heard Ontario's international-liquidity reference in October 2026; outcome pending and details not verified here).

Risks to the vertical are regulatory rather than demand-side: mandatory RG tools and centralised self-exclusion, a prohibition on marketing that 'promotes excessive play' or implies skill affects outcomes, game-certification throughput via accredited test facilities, and the political temperature around gambling harm (the Premier wants operators to fund treatment). None of these change the conclusion that casino — not sports — is the profit pool in Alberta.

segments.name: Legacy market: Play Alberta, land-based & lottery
segments.headline: A C$1.5bn-net-income AGLC estate now competes with — and may be cannibalised by — the open online market; AGLC's dual role and a possible Play Alberta sale are governance overhangs.
narrative: AGLC's FY2024-25 Annual Report records gaming net sales of C$2,133.7m (~$1,524m) and gaming net income of C$1,486.9m (~$1,062m), essentially flat on FY2023-24 (~C$1,486m): slots, online and lottery grew while VLT net sales declined, and the province-wide VLT fleet was replaced. Legal gaming comprises slot terminals in roughly 30 casinos, a provincial VLT network, lottery via the Western Canada Lottery Corporation, bingo, raffles and pull-tickets, plus the state online site PlayAlberta.ca. The Budget 2026 fiscal plan projects AGLC gaming and lottery net income of C$1,577m (~$1,126m) in 2026-27 rising to C$1,635m by 2028-29, with total AGLC net income (gaming, liquor, cannabis) steady at ~C$2.4bn (~$1.7bn) a year.

Play Alberta grew from C$179m of net sales in FY2022-23 to C$235m in FY2023-24 and C$269.9m (~$193m) in FY2024-25 (+15%): casino C$197.3m (73.1%), instants C$27.8m, live dealer C$21.4m, lottery C$15.5m and sports C$8.0m. Government has said the platform captured only ~23–32% of provincial online gambling, which is the origin of the '70% unregulated' figure. Play Alberta continues as AGLC's own brand inside the new market and appears in AiGC's registered-site directory; whether its volumes are consolidated into AiGC's 'operators with an active operating agreement' series is not stated in the report notes and is flagged [unverified].

Two governance features matter for private entrants. First, AGLC is both the regulator of the open market and the operator of a competing brand — a conflict Ontario avoided by separating AGCO and iGO from OLG. Second, legislation tabled in May 2026 would permit the sale of Play Alberta's platform and customer data, which could create a privileged, pre-channelised asset for an acquirer. Land-based licensees, meanwhile, are barred from offering or advertising iGaming inducements and cannot link the Winner's Edge retail loyalty scheme to online play, which protects the retail estate from cross-promotion but blunts omnichannel strategies for casino owners such as Indigenous Gaming Partners, Pure Canadian Gaming and Great Canadian.

Cannibalisation of slots and VLTs by online casino is the unmodelled fiscal risk: Budget 2026 assumes flat-to-rising land-based net income while online NAGGR is already running ~C$680m a year. The 2% of GGR earmarked for First Nations initiatives is separate from the existing land-based First Nations Development Fund arrangements; allocation mechanics have not been published, and Indigenous-owned operators or partnerships may seek a role — a watch item.

segments.name: Licensing, revenue share & fees
segments.headline: Ontario's template with a 3% top-line carve-out: ~22% effective public take, C$150k/site/year, 18+, and a 'net revenue' base that is not publicly defined.
narrative: The legal architecture rests on the iGaming Alberta Act (SA 2025; Bill 48, passed spring 2025 and brought into force in January 2026) and amendments to the Gaming, Liquor and Cannabis Act (RSA 2000). Because section 207 of the Criminal Code reserves the conduct and management of lottery schemes to provinces, AiGC — a Government of Alberta corporate enterprise — is the legal operator of every 'Eligible iGame' and private brands are contracted suppliers under commercial operating agreements, exactly as iGaming Ontario contracts operators. AGLC registers operators and suppliers, sets the Standards and Requirements for Internet Gaming (SRIG; ~85 pages published 14 Jan 2026 and revised 18 Jun 2026 to absorb the advertising rules) and enforces them with fines up to loss of registration.

Entry is a three-part AGLC application — corporate and personal due diligence, a compliance/attestation package, and technical integration with the centralised Self-Exclusion Program — followed by a negotiated AiGC agreement; wagers and deposits may be accepted only after AiGC notifies the registrant. Registration opened 13 Jan 2026, the market launched 13 Jul 2026 and the three-month transition for grey-market sites ended 13 Oct 2026. Registration is per distinct iGaming site, so multi-skin groups pay per brand. The published fee schedule: C$50,000 (~$36k) one-time, non-refundable operator application fee that includes due-diligence costs; C$150,000 (~$107k) non-refundable annual registration per site; C$15,000 (~$11k) a year for platform providers and critical gaming systems; C$3,000 (~$2k) a year for 'other' suppliers (e-wallets, oddsmakers, independent integrity monitors, accredited testing facilities); no supplier application fee. Registration is annual; there are no local-ownership, local-server or local-partner requirements in any source reviewed.

The public take is not levied by a tax statute but embedded in the AiGC agreements. The Government of Alberta states that 3% of gross gaming revenue is allocated first — 2% to First Nations initiatives and 1% to social-responsibility and problem-gambling programmes — and that the remaining 'net iGaming revenue' is split 80% to operators and 20% to the province. On a GGR base that is an effective ~22.4% public take (our estimate). Two things are unverified and should be diligenced in the agreement: whether 'net' is struck after promotional credits/bonuses (AiGC's public metric is explicitly 'non-adjusted'), and the treatment of federal GST on gaming supplies. Players face no withholding; recreational gambling winnings are not taxed in Canada.

Against Ontario, Alberta runs the same 20% headline but adds the 3% carve-out, sets a higher per-site registration fee (Ontario's AGCO fee is lower per site [not re-verified here]), lowers the age to 18, and launched with centralised self-exclusion and inducement/athlete advertising limits already in force (Ontario added its athlete restrictions in 2024 and still lacks a centralised exclusion scheme). Roster depth differs too: Ontario's first year ended with 45 operators and 76 sites; Alberta stands at 29 operators and 50 sites after three months with AiGC guiding to 60+ sites in 2027.

Government's own fiscal anchor is a C$76m (~$54m) year-one take, which back-solves to ~C$390m of GGR; applying the published formula to Q3's NAGGR yields ~C$27.4m (~$19.6m) in 80 days and ~C$12.7m in September alone (~C$152m annualised), so the forecast looks conservative by roughly half — mirroring Ontario's early under-forecasting. For an operator the licence cost is immaterial (C$150k is ~0.5% of the annualised September NAGGR of an average-sized licensee); the binding items are the revenue-share base, GST, promotional intensity and marketing rules.

segments.name: Advertising, responsible gambling, payments & enforcement
segments.headline: Day-one rules are the tightest in Canada and the Premier has signalled they may tighten further; enforcement against the offshore 70% is unproven.
narrative: AGLC's 18 Jun 2026 SRIG update moved iGaming advertising from regulation into standards and set the current rulebook, summarised by AiGC on 4 Aug 2026: no advertising or marketing of inducements, bonuses or credits except on the operator's own registered site or in direct communications to players who have given express consent; no targeting of minors, self-excluded or otherwise vulnerable people; no cartoons, influencers or celebrities likely to appeal to minors; no billboards near schools or youth venues; active or retired athletes only in responsible-gambling messaging; no claims that gambling is a route to financial security, that skill alters RNG outcomes, or that encourage chasing losses or 'excessive play'. Licensees are accountable for affiliates, including where a partner also promotes unlicensed sites, and land-based casino licensees may not offer or advertise iGaming inducements. Non-compliance carries fines or loss of registration.

The political direction is toward more restriction, not less. On 26 Jul 2026 Premier Danielle Smith said gambling websites should pay for addiction treatment; on 25 Oct 2026 she said Albertans had complained about being 'bombarded' with gambling ads and that rule changes may be coming. Plausible instruments include volume or watershed limits on broadcast and in-venue advertising, sports-broadcast caps, mandatory RG-message share, or a higher RG levy than the current 1% of GGR. Operators should front-load brand investment now and budget for a rule change in H1 2027.

Responsible-gambling architecture is comparatively strong: a centralised self-exclusion system that lets a person block all iGaming sites, all land-based venues, or all gambling in one step was live at launch and is a condition of registration; 1% of GGR funds RG and treatment (≈C$1.2m from Q3, ≈C$0.6m in September alone on our estimate); limit-setting and RG tools are mandated by SRIG; the minimum age is 18. KYC/AML runs to FINTRAC standards, with sanctions screening, account-sharing detection and continuous geolocation monitoring expected of operators.

On payments, AiGC publishes no deposit-method or transaction data, so market-level figures are n/a. Payment processors and e-wallets must register with AGLC as 'supplier–other' (C$3,000/yr), which gives the regulator a lever over the rails. Canadian regulated iGaming is Interac e-Transfer-led with debit/credit cards, Apple/Google Pay and Paysafe-type wallets secondary [industry norm; not quantified by any regulator source]; SRIG's specific position on credit-card deposits and on crypto (Stake entered via a Canadian entity, Stake Canada Ltd) was not verified in this research and should be confirmed in the standards.

Enforcement is the open question. With the transition closed on 13 Oct 2026, unregistered sites must stop accepting Alberta wagers; AGLC says it will monitor and take action, and AiGC's CEO says the corporation 'has levers' of its own, but neither has published a toolkit (payment blocking, ISP blocking, affiliate or ad-platform liability, legal action). Ontario's experience suggests channelisation stalls in the 80–85% range without active payment and advertising enforcement; Alberta's 70%/75% targets are achievable only if AGLC is seen to act against named holdouts in the next two quarters.

highlights.text: Scale and ramp: NAGGR of C$122.1m (~$87.2m) in 80 days with September at C$56.6m (+30.7% MoM) annualising ~C$680m — about 1.7x the GGR implied by government's C$76m year-one take — before the roster has filled (24 active of 29 approved operators) and before NHL/NFL peak months.

Casino-led profit pool: 78% of NAGGR from RNG casino at a steady ~4.2% hold, an 18+ age floor and a high-income province give higher-LTV, lower-volatility economics than sports-led markets; live casino is under-indexed at 5% and a clear gap for specialists.

Low fiscal drag: ~22.4% effective public take (20% of net + 3% GGR carve-out, est.), C$150,000/site/year (~0.5% of an average licensee's annualised NAGGR), no supplier application fees, no local-ownership or server rules, no player withholding — cheaper than Pennsylvania/Michigan-style iCasino rates and most European multi-tier regimes.

Channelisation runway: ~70% of online play was offshore pre-launch; AiGC targets 70% regulated after year one and 75% by year two, the grace period closed 13 Oct 2026 and affiliates/payment providers sit inside AGLC's registration perimeter — tailwinds for licensed brands if enforcement is visible.

Product white space: Fantasy Sports and Peer-to-Peer (exchange betting, poker) are already eligible categories with zero reported activity, and live dealer's share is falling as RNG brands launch — first movers can own these verticals.

Ontario-compatible compliance stack and transparent monthly regulator data (Excel, third week of each month) cut entry cost for operators already live in Ontario; the 22-sites-on-day-one launch shows AGLC/AiGC can process registrations at pace.
Seasonal lift ahead: NFL mid-season, the NHL (Oilers, Flames) and the Grey Cup in Calgary on 15 Nov 2026 should lift Q4 sportsbook handle and push hold toward 7–8% from Q3's 6.2%.

lowlights.text: Advertising clampdown risk: Premier Smith (25 Oct 2026) said Albertans are complaining about ad saturation and rules may change; with inducement ads already banned, the next step is volume/watershed or sports-broadcast limits — hitting late entrants' ability to build brand.

Crowded field and hidden promo burn: 50 approved sites for a ~5m-person province; because bonuses can only be pushed on-site/CRM, acquisition costs are invisible in AiGC's 'non-adjusted' GGR, so operator net revenue is likely 20–35% below reported NAGGR in year one (estimate).

Regulator-operator conflict: AGLC both regulates the market and runs the competing Play Alberta brand, and May 2026 legislation could enable a sale of Play Alberta's platform/customer data — a privileged, pre-channelised asset for whoever buys it.

Opaque revenue-share base: 'net iGaming revenue' is not publicly defined (promo deductibility, GST treatment unknown) and the 3% GGR carve-out is a top-line levy regardless of margin; the government's own C$76m forecast is already stale, inviting a re-cut of the split if the take overshoots.

Sports economics are thin and volatile: betting is only 16% of NAGGR with hold swinging 4.6% (Aug) to 7.3% (Sep); sports-first entrants without casino cross-sell face marginal unit economics under a ~22% take and tight marketing rules.

Data limitations: figures are unaudited, NAGGR is pre-promotion, 'active accounts' are not unique players and no operator-level data is published — share tracking and penetration analysis are impossible from regulator data alone.

Legal and federal overhangs: the Supreme Court of Canada's pending ruling on Ontario's international liquidity-pooling reference governs whether P2P poker/DFS can pool beyond Alberta; US-style prediction-market contracts are outside the Act with no stated AGLC position; and the Premier's push for operators to fund addiction treatment could translate into a higher RG levy.

forecast.intro: The 'guidance bridge' here is fiscal: Minister Nally's year-one forecast of C$76m (~$54m) in provincial proceeds implied ~C$390m of first-year GGR, whereas the regulator's first three months printed C$122.1m of NAGGR with September at C$56.6m — a run-rate that, through the published 3%-then-20% formula, yields ~C$12.7m of public take per month (~C$152m annualised). Third-party estimates attributed to H2 Gambling Capital (C$850m to C$1.2bn year-one GGR; conflicting, unverified at source) bracket the upside. Our own 12-month estimate (13 Jul 2026–12 Jul 2027) is C$740–810m of NAGGR assuming 3–5% monthly growth as the roster expands from 24 to ~40 live sites and offshore volume channelises, implying public take of ~C$165–180m — more than double budget.

Q3-26 actual NAGGR (80 days)
bridge.change: 31% of implied FY1 GGR in 22% of the year

forecast.view: **Revenue:** we expect monthly NAGGR of C$75–90m by mid-2027 (estimate), with casino holding 75–80% of the mix, sports oscillating 15–20% by season and live casino recovering toward 7–8% as specialists launch; active accounts should pass 500,000 by Q1 2027 but ARPPA will plateau near C$150–170 as lower-value sports accounts dilute the base. **Margins:** operator net revenue will trail NAGGR by 20–35% in year one on launch promotions, then converge as the inducement-ad ban caps above-the-line spend; the ~22% effective take, GST and C$150k/site leave mid-teens EBITDA margins achievable only for top-eight-share operators — expect exits or skin consolidation among the 50 approved sites from H2 2027. **Rules:** the direction of travel is tighter, not looser — we assign a high probability to new advertising volume/placement limits in H1 2027, a meaningful probability of a higher RG levy or treatment-funding obligation, and a decision on Play Alberta's future (sale or repositioning) within 12 months; the revenue split itself is unlikely to be reopened before the first annual AiGC report, but an over-delivering take versus budget raises the risk. **Enforcement** against named offshore holdouts in the next two quarters is the single biggest determinant of whether the 70%/75% channelisation targets — and the upside half of our range — are met.
watch: October 2026 Market Performance Report (due third week of November): first full month after the 13 Oct grace-period close — look for operator count moving from 24 toward 29+, sports share with NFL/NHL, and whether Fantasy/P2P appear.
Premier Smith's advertising review: any AGLC bulletin or SRIG amendment on ad volume, watershed or sports-broadcast limits (H1 2027 risk window) and any change to the 1% RG allocation.
AGLC enforcement actions against unregistered sites, payment processors or affiliates — the credibility test for 70%/75% channelisation.
Play Alberta: progress of the May 2026 bill enabling a sale of the platform/customer data, and whether AiGC clarifies if Play Alberta volumes are inside its reported series.
Supreme Court of Canada decision on Ontario's international liquidity-pooling reference — determines P2P poker/DFS viability in Alberta.
Alberta Budget 2027 (Feb 2027): first official iGaming revenue line against the C$76m forecast, and any sign of land-based slot/VLT cannibalisation in AGLC's net-income forecast.
Definition and audit of the revenue-share base (promo deductibility, GST) in AiGC's first annual report; First Nations 2% allocation mechanics.
Roster additions toward Keene's 60+ sites and early consolidation signals among sub-scale skins.
